sections.title: Command-Line & Software Tools
sections.content:
ping — tests reachability + round-trip time (ICMP echo). ping 127.0.0.1 tests the local stack.
traceroute / tracert — shows the hop-by-hop path and where latency/loss starts.
ipconfig (Windows) / ip / ifconfig (Linux) — view/renew IP config; ipconfig /all shows DHCP/DNS; /release and /renew.
nslookup / dig — query DNS records to diagnose name resolution.
arp -a — view the IP-to-MAC table.
netstat — active connections and listening ports; ss on Linux.
nmap — scan hosts/ports and discover devices.
tcpdump / Wireshark — capture and inspect packets (protocol analyzer).
pathping / mtr — combine ping + traceroute over time.
Speed test / iperf — measure throughput.
exam_tips: ping tests reachability; traceroute/tracert shows the path and where it breaks.
nslookup/dig diagnose DNS; ipconfig /all shows the DHCP/DNS a host received.
Wireshark/tcpdump capture packets; nmap scans ports/hosts.

sections.title: Diagnosing Service Issues
sections.content:
DNS problems — can ping an IP but not a name = DNS. Check the resolver, records, and TTL; flush the cache; try nslookup.
DHCP problems — a 169.254.x.x (APIPA) address means no DHCP response; check scope exhaustion, the relay/IP helper, and reachability to the server.
Gateway/routing — can reach the local subnet but not remote = default gateway or routing issue (traceroute to find where it stops).
Time (NTP) — bad clocks break certificates/TLS and Kerberos auth.
Name vs IP test isolates the layer: if the IP works but the name doesn't, it's DNS; if neither works, it's connectivity/routing.
Blocked ports / firewall/ACL — service up but unreachable on its port; verify rules and test with telnet/Test-NetConnection to the port.
exam_tips: Ping by IP works but by name fails → DNS problem.
Reach local but not remote hosts → default gateway / routing problem.

sections.title: Performance Issues
sections.content:
Latency — delay (ms); high latency hurts real-time apps. Jitter — variation in latency; ruins VoIP/video. Packet loss — dropped packets cause retransmits and choppy media.
Bottlenecks — a saturated link, overloaded device CPU, or duplex mismatch. Check interface utilization and error/discard counters.
Bandwidth vs throughput — the pipe size vs what you actually get. Congestion and contention reduce throughput; apply QoS.
Wireless performance — low RSSI, interference, co-channel overlap, too many clients per AP, or wrong band.
Common causes: duplex/speed mismatch (collisions), MTU/fragmentation issues, failing hardware, broadcast storms, and asymmetrical routing.
Fix: baseline, isolate the segment, check errors, and correct the specific bottleneck.
exam_tips: Jitter (varying latency) and packet loss degrade VoIP/video — mitigate with QoS.
A duplex mismatch causes collisions, errors, and very low throughput.
Rising interface errors/discards point to a physical or duplex/speed problem.

concept_cards.hook: A tool using ICMP echo to test reachability and round-trip time to a host; pinging 127.0.0.1 tests the local TCP/IP stack.
Shows the hop-by-hop path to a destination and reveals where latency or packet loss begins.
Command-line tools that query DNS records to diagnose name-resolution problems.
Software that captures and inspects packets to diagnose protocol-level issues; tcpdump is the CLI equivalent.
A host with a 169.254.x.x address never reached a DHCP server — the clue points to a DHCP or connectivity failure.
Variation in packet latency; high jitter degrades real-time traffic like VoIP and video even when average latency is fine.
Packets that never arrive, forcing retransmissions and causing choppy audio/video and slow transfers.
Bandwidth is the link's theoretical capacity; throughput is the actual data rate achieved after overhead, congestion, and errors.

practice_questions.q: A host can ping 8.8.8.8 but cannot reach www.example.com. What is the likely issue?
practice_questions.explanation: Reaching an IP but not a name points to DNS; the connectivity itself works.

practice_questions.q: VoIP calls are choppy though average latency is low. Which metric is most likely the culprit?
practice_questions.explanation: Jitter (variation in latency) degrades real-time audio even when average latency looks fine.

practice_questions.q: Which command shows the full hop-by-hop path to a destination and where latency appears?
practice_questions.explanation: traceroute/tracert lists each hop and its round-trip time, revealing where the path degrades.

practice_questions.q: A PC shows a 169.254.x.x address. What failed?
options: It could not reach a DHCP server (APIPA)
practice_questions.explanation: A 169.254 APIPA address means no DHCP server responded.

practice_questions.q: Rising interface error and discard counters most likely indicate what?
options: A physical or duplex/speed problem on the link
practice_questions.explanation: Error/discard counters climb from cabling, duplex mismatch, or failing hardware at the physical layer.

practice_questions.q: Which tool captures and inspects individual packets for deep analysis?
practice_questions.explanation: Wireshark (or tcpdump on the CLI) captures packets for protocol-level troubleshooting.

practice_questions.q: A host reaches other devices on its own subnet but nothing remote. What is the likely cause?
options: Bad patch cable to the PC
practice_questions.explanation: Local works but remote fails points to the default gateway or a routing issue.

practice_questions.q: A gigabit link only achieves ~10 Mbps with many late collisions. What is the likely cause?
practice_questions.explanation: A duplex mismatch (one full, one half) causes late collisions and drastically reduced throughput.

practice_questions.q: Which command on Windows shows the DHCP server and DNS servers a host received?
practice_questions.explanation: ipconfig /all displays full IP configuration including DHCP server and DNS servers.

practice_questions.q: nslookup resolves names fine, but the browser can't load any site, while pinging IPs works. What next?
options: Check the proxy/firewall or the application, not DNS or connectivity
practice_questions.explanation: If DNS resolves and IPs ping, name resolution and L1–L3 are fine; look higher (proxy/app/port filtering).
